Black Horse
BLAK HORS
n. phr. (the third horse of the seals, and the horses of Zechariah's chariots)
English black, Old English blaec, rendering Greek melas in Revelation 6:5 and Hebrew shachor in Zechariah 6:2. The colour carries famine and mourning in Hebrew usage.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version uses the phrase in two prophets. In the Revelation the third seal brings it: “And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third beast say, Come and see. And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand.” The balances are scales, and the voice that follows prices wheat and barley at a day's wage for a day's bread while charging the rider to spare the oil and the wine. This is not famine as total crop failure but famine as ruinous scarcity, where food is available and unaffordable and the luxuries of the rich are untouched. It is a judgment that falls hardest on the poor, and the detail about the oil and the wine is a moral detail, not a botanical one. In Zechariah the black horses are among the teams of the four chariots that come from between two mountains of brass: “In the first chariot were red horses; and in the second chariot black horses.” These are the horses of God's patrols, and the black team goes out with a commission — “The black horses which are therein go forth into the north country” — the north being the quarter from which Israel's conquerors had come. In both prophets the colour is bound to want and to mourning, and in both the horse is under orders.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Black, of the colour of night; destitute of light; figuratively, dismal, mournful, calamitous. A black horse, Revelation 6:5, the horse of famine, whose rider bears a pair of balances.

Black, of the colour of night; destitute of light or whiteness.

Figuratively, dismal, gloomy, sorrowful, calamitous.

A black horse, Revelation 6:5, bearing a rider with a pair of balances.

Hebrew shachor, black, of the horses of the second chariot, Zechariah 6:2.

The black horses go forth into the north country, Zechariah 6:6.

Key Scripture

Rev 6:5 — "And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third beast say, Come and see. And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand."

Rev 6:6 — "And I heard a voice in the midst of the four beasts say, A measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny; and see thou hurt not the oil and the wine."

Zec 6:2 — "In the first chariot were red horses; and in the second chariot black horses;"

Zec 6:6 — "The black horses which are therein go forth into the north country; and the white go forth after them; and the grisled go forth toward the south country."

Modern Corruption

The third seal is read as undifferentiated disaster, when the balances and the sparing of the oil and the wine make it a judgment specifically upon an economy that prices bread beyond the poor.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The failure here is a failure of attention to detail that Scripture has taken trouble to supply. The third seal is routinely summarised as “famine” and left there, which loses the balances. A pair of scales in a rider's hand is an instrument of commerce, and the voice that follows does not announce that there is no food; it announces a price. A measure of wheat for a penny, with a penny the day's wage of Matthew 20:2, is a day's labour for a day's bread and nothing over. The oil and the wine — the goods of the comfortable — are expressly spared. Scripture is describing a scarcity that sorts men by what they can pay.

The principle to recover is that God's judgments are discriminating and that Scripture's concern for just weights is of a piece with this vision. The law repeatedly forbids a false balance and the Proverbs call it an abomination; here a balance appears in the hand of a judgment-rider, and the bread of the poor is weighed out. Zechariah's black team, sent into the north country, makes the same point from the other side: these horses are patrols under orders, not accidents. The reader is meant to see both that such scarcity is a real visitation and that the hand that opened the seal is the Lamb's.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek melas, black; Hebrew shachor, black; the colour of famine and mourning; the rider bears zugos, a pair of balances.

expand to see more

Greek melas, black, Revelation 6:5.

Greek zugos, a yoke, hence a beam and so a pair of balances or scales.

Hebrew shachor, black, of the horses of the second chariot, Zechariah 6:2.

The balances mark scarcity priced, not food absent, Revelation 6:6.

The oil and the wine are spared, marking a judgment that sorts by wealth.
